questions.prompt: Dipalmitoylphosphatidylcholine (DPPC) is the primary surface-tension-reducing phospholipid found in pulmonary surfactant.
In patients with restrictive lung diseases, such as interstitial fibrosis, lung compliance is characteristically increased.
According to Henry's Law, the amount of oxygen physically dissolved in the plasma is directly proportional to the partial pressure of oxygen (P_(O2)).
During moderate exercise, physiological dead space typically decreases because the increase in pulmonary blood flow improves the ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) match in the upper lobes.
In the healthy human lung, the greatest portion of total airway resistance is located in the small bronchioles (diameter < 2mm).
The oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve for fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is shifted to the right of the adult curve to facilitate oxygen delivery to fetal tissues.
Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE) is primarily located on the luminal surface of the pulmonary capillary endothelium.
Central chemoreceptors on the medulla are directly stimulated by a decrease in arterial P_(O2) below 60 mmHg.
In the "chloride shift" occurring in systemic tissues, chloride ions move into the erythrocyte to maintain electrical neutrality as bicarbonate ions diffuse out.
The Bohr equation is the standard physiological method used to calculate the volume of the anatomical dead space.
In Zone 3 of the upright lung, pulmonary arterial pressure is greater than venous pressure, and both exceed the alveolar pressure.
In a tension pneumothorax, the lung on the affected side collapses inward while the chest wall tends to expand or recoil outward.
Carbon monoxide (CO) has an affinity for the heme binding sites on hemoglobin that is approximately 20 times greater than that of oxygen.
Total lung capacity (TLC) and residual volume (RV) can be measured using standard simple spirometry.
The P_(50) of the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve represents the partial pressure of oxygen at which 50% of the hemoglobin binding sites are occupied by oxygen.
The initial respiratory response to the hypoxia of high altitude is hyperventilation, which subsequently produces a state of respiratory alkalosis.
The "oxygen cascade" describes the series of steps in which the partial pressure of oxygen increases as it moves from the atmosphere to the mitochondria.
In emphysema, the "scooped-out" appearance of the expiratory flow-volume curve is caused by the dynamic compression and premature closure of airways lacking radial traction.
The Bohr effect states that a decrease in blood pH or an increase in P_(CO2) shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the right, decreasing hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen.
Pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) reaches its lowest point when the lung volume is at the functional residual capacity (FRC).
The respiratory exchange ratio (R) is numerically higher when the body is primarily oxidizing lipids compared to when it is oxidizing carbohydrates.
Juxtacapillary (J) receptors are sensory nerve endings in the alveolar walls that are stimulated by pulmonary capillary engorgement or interstitial edema.
Alveolar ventilation is calculated by subtracting the anatomical dead space from the tidal volume and multiplying the result by the respiratory rate.
In the upright lung, the ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) ratio is highest at the base of the lung and lowest at the apex.
Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction (HPV) is a local mechanism that diverts blood flow away from poorly ventilated alveoli to maintain optimal gas exchange.
The carotid bodies are peripheral chemoreceptors that respond to a decrease in arterial P_(O2), an increase in P_(CO2), and a decrease in pH.
Polycythemia, an increase in red blood cell count, is a long-term adaptation to high altitude mediated by the renal release of erythropoietin.
Inspiratory capacity is defined as the maximum volume of gas that can be inspired starting from the end-expiratory level (FRC).
In an upright person, the intrapleural pressure at the base of the lung is more negative (more subatmospheric) than the intrapleural pressure at the apex.
During normal, quiet tidal breathing, expiration is an active process requiring the contraction of the internal intercostal muscles.
The solubility of carbon dioxide in blood is approximately 24 times greater than the solubility of oxygen at 37°C.
Peripheral chemoreceptors are the only sensors responsible for the immediate increase in ventilation in response to a metabolic acidosis.
In a patient with severe iron-deficiency anemia, the percentage saturation of the available hemoglobin remains normal if the Pa_(O2) is 100 mmHg.
According to the Law of Laplace, for a constant surface tension, the pressure required to keep an alveolus open increases as the radius of the alveolus decreases.
The methacholine challenge test is used clinically to confirm airway hyperresponsiveness by inducing bronchoconstriction in susceptible patients.
An arterial blood gas result showing a pH of 7.25 and a Pa_(CO2) of 60 mmHg is consistent with a state of acute, uncompensated respiratory acidosis.
Hysteresis in the lung's pressure-volume relationship means that for a given transpulmonary pressure, lung volume is greater during expiration than during inspiration.
The anatomical dead space consists of the volume of the conducting airways, including the trachea, bronchi, and the respiratory bronchioles.
In a patient with a complete intrapulmonary shunt (V/Q = 0), the systemic arterial P_(O2) will never reach the level of the inspired P_(O2), regardless of the Fi_(O2).
Stimulation of the parasympathetic fibers in the vagus nerve leads to bronchodilation and a decrease in total airway resistance.
An increase in the concentration of 2,3-diphosphoglycerate (2,3-DPG) in erythrocytes shifts the oxyhemoglobin dissociation curve to the left.
Physiological dead space is a functional measurement that is always greater than or equal to the anatomical dead space.
In an upright person, both ventilation and perfusion are quantitatively greater at the base of the lung than at the apex.
A widened alveolar-arterial (A-a) P_(O2) gradient is expected in a healthy individual who is hypoventilating due to a drug overdose.
Peripheral chemoreceptors in the carotid bodies respond specifically to the partial pressure of oxygen (Pa_(O2)) rather than the total oxygen content of the blood.
Fetal hemoglobin has a higher affinity for oxygen because it binds the allosteric effector 2,3-DPG less strongly than adult hemoglobin A.
If a patient develops a large pulmonary embolism, the V/Q ratio in the affected, non-perfused lung units becomes zero.
The intrapleural pressure becomes less negative (moves toward zero) as a person inhales from FRC toward total lung capacity.
The rate of diffusion for a gas across the blood-gas barrier is directly proportional to the surface area and inversely proportional to the thickness of the barrier.
The dorsal respiratory group (DRG), located in the medulla, contains primarily inspiratory neurons that provide the basic rhythm for breathing.
